summary: In Greek mythology, Actaeus (Ancient Greek Ἀκταῖος, "coast-man"), also called Actaeon in some late notices, was the first king of Attica according to Pausanias. He ruled the land then named Acte or Actica; after his death Cecrops received the kingdom as his son-in-law. Distinct from Actaeon the hunter of Artemis, grandson of Cadmus.
etymology: Ancient Greek Ἀκταῖος (Aktaîos), "coast-man," from aktē ("coast, shore"); the land-name Acte / Actica precedes Cecropia and Attica in Pausanias and the Parian Chronicle.

sections.heading: First king of Acte
paragraphs: Pausanias opens the Attic succession with Actaeus as the first to reign over what is now Attica. When he died, Cecrops took the kingdom as Actaeus' son-in-law; Cecrops' daughters Herse, Aglaurus, and Pandrosus, and the short-lived son Erysichthon, follow in that telling. The Parian Chronicle likewise has Actaeus give Aktike its name before Cecrops renamed it Cecropia.

Apollodorus makes earth-born Cecrops the first king who renamed Acte Cecropia, yet still records that Cecrops married Agraulus (Aglaurus), daughter of Actaeus — preserving the older house in genealogy even where the Bibliotheca does not count Actaeus among the kings.

sections.heading: Family and homonym care
paragraphs: Actaeus' daughters include Aglaurus (wife of Cecrops) and, in some late notices, Erse, Pandrosos, and a virgin Phoenice after whom Scamon of Mytilene said the Phoenician letters were named. His wife is obscure.
The atlas id actaeus-athens is this Attic king alone. He is not Actaeon (Aktaion) the hunter whom Artemis turned into a stag — a Cadmean grandson of a different generation and myth.
